input: Turning to the question of the absorber wall, the thickness that results once the corrosion allowance has been added is 77 mm, and this is the figure that should be carried forward for the shell. It is worth emphasising that the stated thickness is a final thickness rather than a pre-allowance figure, since the allowance has already been included in arriving at it. The stated thickness is for the absorber shell; the lean solvent pump casing is outside the comparison that follows. With regard to the gasket selection, the two candidate materials have been compared on the basis of temperature limit only, and on that basis the material with the higher temperature limit is to be preferred. No other property has been brought into the comparison, and the preference should not be read as a judgement on the materials in any broader sense. It is, admittedly, a narrow basis for a selection, but it is the basis that has been adopted here, and the preference follows from it directly: where the temperature limits differ, the higher-rated material is the one that is preferred, and the lower-rated material is set aside for this duty. It may also be observed that the inclusion of the allowance at this stage is deliberate, since it avoids the confusion that can arise when a thickness is quoted in one place without the allowance and in another place with it, and the reader is left unsure which figure is intended to govern. The preference between the gaskets is likewise deliberately narrow in its stated basis. The argument on this point is not yet complete, since the consequences of the choice for the adjoining parts of the design remain to be worked through, but the thickness figure and the direction of the gasket preference are as stated above.
target: The absorber wall thickness is 77 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The stated thickness is the final thickness, not a pre-allowance figure: the allowance is inside the number, and no further addition is made when the shell is specified. The stated thickness is for the absorber shell; the lean solvent pump casing is outside the comparison. Two gasket materials are compared on temperature limit only. The material with the higher temperature limit is preferred. No other property enters the comparison, and the preference is not a judgement on the two materials in any wider sense: it rests on the temperature limit, and it stands while the temperature limit remains the deciding criterion for the joint. A gasket choice made on a single property is narrow, and the narrowness is stated rather than hidden: chemical behaviour, compressibility, and relaxation do not appear in the argument, because the comparison as set up admits the temperature limit alone. Within that frame, the ordering of the two materials is direct. The higher-rated material is taken, and the lower-rated material is set aside for this duty. The corrosion allowance is part of the duty the wall has to meet, not an addition made for comfort: the shell loses material in service, and the thickness at the end of the interval between inspections is the thickness that has to resist the pressure. Stating the thickness with the allowance inside it prevents the error of adding the allowance twice, once in the design figure and once again at ordering. The gasket preference has a parallel discipline: because the comparison admits one property, the preference cannot be transferred to a joint whose deciding criterion is different. The wall result and the gasket preference are separate conclusions: the thickness closes the shell sizing with its allowance included, and the preference orders the gasket materials on the one property the comparison allows, and the argument continues from those two fixed points.
